I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging.
  • Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
  • When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the organization’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

In a recent development, the ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

In a recent development, of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Recent findings suggest that instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

It has been revealed that plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

It has been revealed that the battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be swiftly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

It has been revealed that and that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as swiftly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

It has been revealed that but clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

In a recent development, I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

It has been revealed that now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • In a recent development, you log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible.
  • While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, you log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even challenges with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” claims Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.).

According to recent reports, but proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” notes Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

Sources indicate that while everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

According to recent reports, martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

According to recent reports, at over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

Read more: Best Home Office Chairs.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that crucial feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

Industry observers note that while some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Read More: Best Home Office Chairs.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

Industry observers note that WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she states, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”.

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

It has been revealed that her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

It has been revealed that this walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

It has been revealed that not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is crucial because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.).

Industry observers note that at the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

According to recent reports, it’s notable to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. We also considered how stable each setup felt, how easily it fit into a home office, and any drawbacks our testers encountered.

New Bitcoin Core Revision: Breaking Down the Details

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (448 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the key reason behind the setup is error handling in a way where there's no break in wallet usage that needs manual intervention in the process, to a significant degree.
  • Industry observers note that the pull request follows two earlier fixes, one for unnamed legacy wallets and another for crashes when Bitcoin Core couldn't write to the wallet directory, on the whole.
  • This isn't the first fix for wallet migration either, in the actual application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the key reason behind the setup is error handling in a way where there's no break in wallet usage that needs manual intervention in the process, to a significant degree. Indeed, a Bitcoin wallet migration change was, broadly speaking, merged on November 25 by Bitcoin Core.

Industry observers note that the pull request follows two earlier fixes, one for unnamed legacy wallets and another for crashes when Bitcoin Core couldn't write to the wallet directory, on the whole. In fact, the thinking is to handle failures in a controlled way so the process can (to some degree) automatically restore the original wallet without needing manual intervention.

This isn't the first fix for wallet migration either, in the actual application.

In a recent development, some mismatches during wallet creation could crash the graphical app or cause it to return a generic error. Those differences are now caught by Bitcoin Core and reported, which lets the migration process restore the original wallet from its backup, There are a couple of cases where the process could abruptly stop.

Recent findings suggest that trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory could also throw an error and skip cleanup, in real-world scenarios. In fact, now the process crashes with a clear error message. The test for this case is checking that the wallet is still in the old database format after the failure.

The biggest change is in how Bitcoin Core moves the wallet to SQLite. Earlier, it deleted the original database before writing the fresh one. If something went wrong while making the new database or writing the wallet records, the user could end up restoring the backup by hand.

In a recent development, now Bitcoin Core builds the SQLite database next to the original. So, the old database stays in place. These days, the upcoming one is being built. Once the wallet records have been written successfully, Bitcoin Core can move the new database into place. The pull request also tests this with a wallet stored on a separate filesystem.

Industry observers note that A leftover SQLite journal in the wallet directory can corrupt the new database if SQLite uses it for the migrated wallet. In fact, Bitcoin Core now stops the migration when it finds a file, and the test checks that the journal stays in place. Moreover, the wallet keeps its legacy format.

Industry observers note that it's significant to keep in mind that automatic recovery still hinges on the backup being copied back successfully. As Ryan Ofsky mentioned in his review, if that copy crashes, the user still has to restore the backup by hand, on the whole.

Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested.
  • And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
  • The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the tech giant started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the tech giant started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

Sources indicate that the key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

In a recent development, then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

According to recent reports, tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make at the moment, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab debuts on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Recent findings suggest that yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

It has been revealed that tesla’s answer to all those owners is a fresh car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

Sources indicate that you don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if people join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

In a recent development, and the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?
